title: MDCAT Past Papers: What Changed With the New Syllabus
excerpt: Not every MDCAT past paper reflects the current exam — the test has changed format more than once in recent years. Here's how to tell which past papers are still useful and which need to be used carefully.

content.text: Why "just do past papers" isn't quite enough advice

Every MDCAT prep guide tells you to practice with past papers, and it's good advice — but it comes with an asterisk that often gets left out. MDCAT hasn't looked the same every year. The test has gone through more than one structural change recently, which means a past paper from several years ago may not test the same number of questions, the same subject balance, or even the same sections as the exam you're about to sit.

Using an old past paper without knowing what's changed can leave you with a distorted sense of how much time to spend per subject, or missing practice on a section that didn't exist in earlier versions of the test at all.

Before working through any past paper, check which year and version it's from, and compare its structure to the current PMDC Uniform Curriculum. A perfect score on an outdated-format paper doesn't tell you as much as you'd think about your current readiness.
The big-picture shifts worth knowing about
Across recent years, MDCAT has changed in a few consistent ways, according to test-prep analysis of the exam's history:

items: The total number of questions has changed between different versions of the test
The exam has moved between computer-based and paper-based formats at different points
Biology's share of the total paper has increased significantly compared to older versions, while English's share has decreased
A Logical Reasoning section was added that didn't exist in earlier versions of the test at all

content.text: The exact question counts and dates for each version of the exam are best confirmed directly from the official PMDC syllabus and past announcements, since different prep sites summarize this history slightly differently. Treat this post as a heads-up to check, not a substitute for the official record.
What this means for using older past papers
If you're working through a past paper from a noticeably older version of the exam, a few things are worth adjusting for:

items: Subject balance is probably off. If Biology's weight has increased over time and English's has decreased, an older paper will under-represent how much Biology matters now and over-represent how much English matters now. Don't calibrate your study time allocation off an old paper's subject balance.

The Logical Reasoning section may be missing entirely. If a past paper predates that section's introduction, you simply won't get practice on it from that paper — you'll need dedicated practice material for it elsewhere.

Timing per question may not translate directly. If the total number of questions or total time has changed between versions, the pace you need to maintain on the current exam isn't the same pace an older past paper would have required.

content.text: What doesn't change as much: the actual content

Here's the reassuring part — while the format and weightage have shifted, the underlying content is still drawn from the same FSc Pre-Medical curriculum it always has been. A well-written Biology or Chemistry question from an older past paper is often still testing a concept you genuinely need to know, even if the overall paper it came from doesn't match the current structure. Older past papers remain useful for content practice and for getting a feel for how MDCAT phrases questions, even in subjects or sections where the exact weighting has shifted.

The safest approach is to prioritize the most recent past papers you can find — ones from the current 180-MCQ, Logical-Reasoning-included format — for building your sense of timing and subject balance, while still using older papers as a secondary source of extra practice questions on core content.
A practical way to use past papers this cycle

items: Start with the most recent available past papers that match the current exam structure, and use these for realistic timed practice
Use older past papers as supplementary question banks for content review, not as a guide to timing or subject weightage
If a source's past paper collection doesn't specify which year or version each paper is from, be cautious about drawing conclusions from it about pacing or subject balance
When in doubt about whether a specific past paper reflects the current format, check the year against the official PMDC syllabus history rather than assuming

content.text: If you're not sure where your own past-paper practice stands relative to what the current exam expects, our merit calculator and subject guides can help you sanity-check where you're spending your remaining time.

Past papers are still one of the most valuable things you can practice with — but only if you know which version of the exam each one reflects. The safest habit is simple: confirm the year and format of any past paper before trusting its subject balance or timing, lean on the most recent papers for realistic practice, and use older ones for extra content drilling rather than as a guide to how the current exam is actually structured.

items.question: Can I use any MDCAT past paper for practice?
items.answer: Not without checking its year and format first. MDCAT has changed structure more than once in recent years — question counts, subject balance, and even entire sections have shifted, so an old past paper may not reflect the current exam.

items.question: What are the main ways MDCAT's format has changed over time?
items.answer: The total number of questions has changed between versions, the exam has moved between computer-based and paper-based formats, Biology's share has increased while English's has decreased, and a Logical Reasoning section was added that didn't exist earlier.

items.question: Are older MDCAT past papers still useful at all?
items.answer: Yes, for content practice — the underlying material is still drawn from the same FSc Pre-Medical curriculum. They're just less reliable for calibrating timing or subject-time allocation, since the overall structure may not match the current exam.

items.question: How do I know if a past paper reflects the current MDCAT format?
items.answer: Check whether it matches the current 180-MCQ format including a Logical Reasoning section. If a source doesn't specify the year or version of its past papers, be cautious about drawing conclusions about pacing or subject balance from it.

items.question: Should I prioritize recent or older past papers?
items.answer: Prioritize the most recent past papers matching the current structure for realistic timed practice and subject balance. Use older papers as a secondary source for extra content questions, not as a guide to timing or weightage.
